title: Cutting Quotas, Not Strategy: Apple Tightens the Screws on Internal AI Spending

content_html:
According to multiple media outlets citing people familiar with the matter, Apple has begun tightening the cost of internal AI tool usage. The most direct change falls on engineers: in October of this year, the daily AI allowance for some engineering teams was cut from $300 to $200, and the company is still studying further reductions. In the future, some engineering teams may have only $100 per day. By comparison, many non-engineering teams had already been operating under a $100 cap, while internally there had been discussions about pushing some teams down to $25 per day. For roles that truly cannot do without a high quota, employees can still apply to executives for additional allowance.

What is being cut is waste, not strategy These budgets are mainly used to cover Token consumption for generative models such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini—engineers, who rely heavily on AI for coding, have always had the highest-tier allowances. Over the past year, Silicon Valley's popular "Token Maxxing" culture has driven usage higher and higher, with some even competing over who used more. To rein in the trend, Apple encourages teams to switch to cheaper models or prioritize AI solutions that run on local devices. As the billing unit for mainstream AI services, tokens mean the more you use, the bigger the bill—and that is exactly where Apple wants to turn the valve. But it is worth noting that the company's overall R&D spending is still rising sharply year over year in fiscal 2026, with AI and infrastructure as the main drivers, suggesting the strategy has not slowed down; it is merely tightening the screws on usage discipline.

The industry enters a time of reckoning This shift from "willing to spend" to "counting the cost" is not unique to Apple. After a year of large-scale expansion, the industry is now starting to ask how much productivity those expenses are actually buying back. Internal views are divided: some believe $300 was already generous and rarely maxed out in practice, so the new rules will have limited impact; others see it as a prelude to broader cost-cutting. With some business units bringing in outside consultants to assess efficiency, speculation about restructuring is quietly rising, though there is currently no evidence that Apple has finalized layoff plans. After the early frenzy, companies are shifting their focus from "how much is being used" to "whether it is worth it"—how to keep operating costs down has become a new shared challenge for the entire industry.
